content: 1. Esomeprazole is an oral proton pump inhibitor (PPI) approved by the FDA for the treatment of acid-mediated conditions such as erosive esophagitis due to gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome. 2. Common side effects of esomeprazole include abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhea, flatulence, nausea, dry mouth (xerostomia), headache, and drowsiness (somnolence). 3. For adults, esomeprazole is indicated for the short-term treatment (4 to 8 weeks) of confirmed erosive esophagitis to promote healing and symptom resolution. If healing is not achieved after the initial course, an additional 4 to 8 weeks of treatment may be considered. 4. In infants aged 1 month to less than 1 year, esomeprazole is indicated for short-term treatment (up to 6 weeks) of erosive esophagitis caused by acid-mediated GERD. 5. Esomeprazole is also indicated for maintaining the healing of erosive esophagitis and preventing symptom recurrence. However, controlled studies for maintenance therapy do not extend beyond 6 months. 6. Esomeprazole is used for the short-term treatment (4 to 8 weeks) of heartburn and other GERD-related symptoms in adults and children aged 1 year or older. 7. Esomeprazole is indicated for reducing the occurrence of gastric ulcers associated with continuous NSAID therapy in patients at risk, such as those aged 60 years or older or with a history of gastric ulcers. 8. In combination with amoxicillin and clarithromycin (triple therapy), esomeprazole is indicated for the eradication of Helicobacter pylori infection and the treatment of duodenal ulcer disease (active or within the past 5 years). Eradication of H. pylori reduces the risk of duodenal ulcer recurrence. 9. For patients who fail H. pylori eradication therapy, susceptibility testing should be performed. If resistance to clarithromycin is detected or susceptibility testing is not feasible, alternative antimicrobial therapy should be initiated. 10. Esomeprazole is indicated for the long-term treatment of pathological hypersecretory conditions, including Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome. 11. Esomeprazole delayed-release capsules should be swallowed whole. For patients who have difficulty swallowing capsules, the granules inside the capsule can be mixed with one tablespoon of applesauce and swallowed immediately without chewing or crushing the granules. 12. For patients with a nasogastric tube, esomeprazole delayed-release capsules can be opened, and the granules mixed with 50 mL of water in a catheter-tipped syringe. The mixture should be delivered through the nasogastric tube into the stomach immediately after preparation. 13. Esomeprazole delayed-release oral suspension should be prepared by mixing the contents of the packet with water (5 mL for 2.5 mg or 5 mg packets; 15 mL for 10 mg, 20 mg, or 40 mg packets). The mixture should be stirred, allowed to thicken for 2 to 3 minutes, and consumed within 30 minutes. 14. Esomeprazole is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to substituted benzimidazoles or any component of the formulation. Hypersensitivity reactions may include anaphylaxis, anaphylactic shock, angioedema, bronchospasm, acute interstitial nephritis, and urticaria. 15. Symptomatic response to esomeprazole therapy does not rule out the presence of gastric malignancy. Long-term use of PPIs, including esomeprazole, has been associated with atrophic gastritis in some cases. 16. Acute interstitial nephritis has been observed in patients taking PPIs, including esomeprazole. This condition may occur at any point during therapy and is generally attributed to an idiopathic hypersensitivity reaction. Esomeprazole should be discontinued if acute interstitial nephritis develops. 17. Long-term daily use of acid-suppressing medications, including esomeprazole, may lead to malabsorption of vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) due to hypoor achlorhydria. Rare cases of vitamin B12 deficiency have been reported in the literature. 18. Published observational studies suggest that PPI therapy, including esomeprazole, may be associated with an increased risk of Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD), particularly in hospitalized patients. This diagnosis should be considered in cases of persistent diarrhea. 19. Patients should use the lowest effective dose and shortest duration of PPI therapy appropriate for their condition to minimize risks such as CDAD and osteoporosis-related fractures. 20. Observational studies suggest that long-term PPI therapy (≥1 year) and high-dose use may increase the risk of fractures of the hip, wrist, or spine. Patients at risk for osteoporosis-related fractures should be managed according to established treatment guidelines. 21. Hypomagnesemia, both symptomatic and asymptomatic, has been reported rarely in patients treated with PPIs for at least 3 months, most often after 1 year of therapy. Serious adverse events include tetany, arrhythmias, and seizures. Magnesium replacement and discontinuation of the PPI are typically required. 22. Concomitant use of esomeprazole with clopidogrel should be avoided. Esomeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, which is necessary for the conversion of clopidogrel to its active metabolite, potentially reducing its antiplatelet effect. 23. Patients taking digoxin concomitantly with esomeprazole should be monitored for potential toxicity. 24. Esomeprazole may reduce the absorption of drugs where gastric pH is a critical determinant of bioavailability, such as ketoconazole, atazanavir, iron salts, erlotinib, and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF). Conversely, it may increase the absorption of drugs like digoxin. 25. Esomeprazole is extensively metabolized in the liver by CYP2C19 and CYP3A4. It is not expected to inhibit other CYP enzymes significantly, and no clinically relevant interactions with drugs metabolized by these enzymes have been observed. 26. In clinical trials, esomeprazole was generally well-tolerated in both shortand long-term use. Common adverse reactions included headache, diarrhea, nausea, flatulence, abdominal pain, constipation, and dry mouth. 27. Rare but serious adverse reactions reported during post-marketing surveillance include agranulocytosis, pancytopenia, hepatic failure, interstitial nephritis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis. 28. Concomitant use of esomeprazole with atazanavir or nelfinavir is not recommended due to significant reductions in plasma concentrations of these antiretroviral drugs, potentially leading to loss of therapeutic effect and drug resistance. 29. Esomeprazole may increase the serum concentrations of saquinavir, necessitating clinical and laboratory monitoring for toxicity. Dose reduction of saquinavir may be required. 30. The clinical relevance of this interaction on organ rejection has not been established.
